### 5.4 What sets the forking token

The task-specification states carry the choice into the forking token (Table 3). Writing the task-specification states of a prompt that names the minority algorithm into its padding twin produced that algorithm in 30 of 30 shared streams on all three mixed units, against 0 to 7 of 30 under the padding twin and 0 to 12 of 30 under a random exchange of matched norm, with every program passing [ARTIFACT:art_MZAfDPVhM6Ui]. The argmax at the forking token flips with it (` Kr` to ` Prim`), and the fork margin moves by 4.87 to 22.12 nats toward the minority, against at most 2.00 nats for the random exchange. The same exchange carries a prohibition: writing a shortest path ban's full-state task-specification activations into a neutral twin moved Dijkstra to correct Bellman-Ford/SPFA in 21 of 30 streams against 0 under a matched random exchange (McNemar 21:0, p = 9.5e-7) [ARTIFACT:art_rMlbrjVB1c__].

| Unit | Padding twin | Forced prompt's states exchanged in | Random exchange, matched norm | Exchange vs twin, discordant pairs (p) | Fork-margin change, exchange / random |
|-|-|-|-|-|-|
| Minimum spanning tree weight (Prim) | 0.23 | 1.00 | 0.40 | 23:0 (1.2e-7) | -4.87 / -1.25 |
| Trapped rain water (two pointers) | 0.13 | 1.00 | 0.13 | 26:0 (1.5e-8) | -5.50 / -2.00 |
| Valid anagram (fixed count array) | 0.00 | 1.00 | 0.00 | 30:0 (9.3e-10) | -22.12 / +0.26 |

Post-training made the fork margins (Figure 4). On identical chat-templated ids, Qwen3-8B's fork margin exceeds Qwen3-8B-Base's by 3.27 nats on the grid task, 13.41 on connected components and 2.11 on shortest path, the three default tasks, and by 1.84 and 1.53 nats on the two mixed units; without chat tokens the gains on the default tasks are 5.31, 11.05 and 2.69 nats, so the template does not produce them [ARTIFACT:art_lzuosbrb34wB]. At 64 ordinary phrasing positions per program the two models differ little: the base model's next-token entropy is higher by 0.23 to 0.34 nats, and the instruct model's token is the base model's top token at 90.6% to 95.3% of phrasing positions on the default tasks. At the forking token, the instruct model's choice is the base model's second or third choice in 20, 17 and 19 of 20 programs. The Jensen-Shannon divergence between the two models is 6 to 10 times larger at the fork than at phrasing positions, but only 1.5 to 1.9 times larger than at phrasing positions matched for base-model entropy, which matches the known concentration of post-training shifts at high-entropy tokens [@Meng2026]. The instruct default is therefore not the base model's average answer: on minimum spanning tree weight the base model's fork distribution, pushed through the instruct model's continuations, would give Prim 0.68 where the instruct model writes Kruskal 0.78.

Reading the choice before the forking token was not possible with the readouts we tried, which fits a decision made at that token. A natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [@Yang2024] named the planned algorithm at end-of-prompt positions in 0 of 112 cases, although at the algorithm-name token itself its explanations named the algorithm 80% to 89% of the time [ARTIFACT:art_dbUtqBjT0tPf]. Gemma Scope sparse autoencoder features [@Lieberum2024] read Gemma's fork log-odds across 120 prompt variants (R-squared 0.66 against 0.18 for a text baseline), but a ridge readout of the raw residual reached 0.72, and clamping features steered the fork less than a difference-in-means direction (+1.78 against +4.04 nats at matched norm) [ARTIFACT:art_zNyBP6zieI5u]. Distributed alignment search at the forking token produced edits that moved the algorithm, but permuted-label and random-initialisation controls kept 0.63 to 0.87 and 0.69 of the effect, so no certified low-rank variable for the algorithm was found [ARTIFACT:art_e-_q5mSJGrSb].

### 5.5 Other controls reweight the same repertoire

Controls other than temperature moved programs among known algorithms when they moved them at all (Table 4). Random context seeds left the default intact: with `seed=d32qxk4nt43` or `seed=(horse chair roof love)` prepended, the grid task stayed BFS in 100 of 100 programs and shortest path Dijkstra in 100 of 100, although the word seed moved the read-position state 1.555 times the paraphrase noise [ARTIFACT:art_UoCVh2Qe5RZ0]. Context with meaning did move the algorithm: a paragraph that implies a relaxation over all edges without naming it turned 61 of 92 correct shortest path programs into Bellman-Ford/SPFA (permutation p < 0.001). Instructions moved claims more than code. "Make a fully novel algorithm never seen before" lowered the Dijkstra share by 14.6 points, toward Bellman-Ford/SPFA. Under two 2,000-word novelty instructions, 84% of outputs claimed a new algorithm, 39% of those contained no code, and 75% of the rest were catalogue algorithms [ARTIFACT:art_ccAbfJVcv0LO]. Asking the model to list ten approaches and implementing one picked at random raised the number of ideas at depth 25 from 1.26 to 3.98 on the grid task and from 1.00 to 3.00 on shortest path, at pass rates of 0.55 and 0.75 [ARTIFACT:art_UoCVh2Qe5RZ0].

Bans relocate the default within the repertoire. A single ban of the default by name lands on one substitute, DFS for BFS and Bellman-Ford/SPFA for Dijkstra, recomputed over all pooled ban samples [ARTIFACT:art__5akZ9W9iZM4]. Banning five grid algorithms at once fails in most models: across ten open configurations only Qwen3-32B with thinking clears the pre-registered 0.20 bar of correct survivors [ARTIFACT:art_R-HSmXq2t97f], and the others keep writing BFS or DFS, often without naming it. Counted by runtime behaviour, lexical compliance exceeded mechanistic compliance by 0.70 pooled over ten configurations, a descriptive figure because the expansion-order tracer failed its gold gate [ARTIFACT:art_8nXdw3_lDAll]. With an exact behavioural instrument on online bin packing, Qwen3-8B without thinking obeyed a five-name ban by name in 0.91 of programs but by mechanism in 0.51 (difference 0.40 [0.21, 0.55]), while Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking left the banned rules [ARTIFACT:art_ZkX7AmcN4vDO].

The audits found no correct novel algorithm under any single-sample control, including 0 of 10,651 correct programs under random pushes [ARTIFACT:art_SHaWv77P1XCI] and 0 of 4,703 in the temperature-law sweeps (rule-of-three bound 0.0006) [ARTIFACT:art_lzuosbrb34wB]. Evaluator-guided search did better than the textbook rule without producing a confirmed new idea. On k-th smallest it produced 78 known techniques outside the catalogue in 2,500 calls against 2 in 500 for the instruction alone, a per-call ratio of 7.8 (lower 95% bound 2.41), all of them published methods [ARTIFACT:art_VhaHGe7SxV95]. On online bin packing the best searched programs reached 1.40% to 2.43% excess bins over the lower bound on held-out Weibull instances against 3.98% for best fit, but none beat the published FunSearch heuristic (0.68%) [ARTIFACT:art_k7A5-5vcXY1g]. One reader classed eight of those programs as a new idea; an independent replication with two new seeds found 0 novel among 40 judged programs [ARTIFACT:art_dq4MiqNM89Go].

### 5.6 Where a five-name ban lands in activation space

The one configuration that obeys the five-name ban moves to unit-weight Dijkstra, and whether that survivor lies at the edge of the banned algorithms or opposite them depends on how the map is built (Figure 5). Qwen3-32B with thinking writes BFS in 91 of 100 baseline programs; under the ban its six correct catalogue survivors are all unit-weight Dijkstra, and on held-out ban templates 9 of 9 are [ARTIFACT:art_R-HSmXq2t97f]. On a map of the ten grid algorithms built from forced prompts that name them (block 31), unit-weight Dijkstra is the non-banned algorithm farthest from the banned five, with a geodesic distance 1.63 times the median of the non-banned algorithms at k = 15 [ARTIFACT:art_VVA3P0ocZNA2]. On a map built from name-scrubbed programs (block 33), it lies at the edge, at 0.67 times the median and nearest to greedy best-first search. Distances on the name-built map track the lexical overlap of the algorithm names (Spearman -0.61 at k = 15) and do not survive a within-algorithm alias test, so names and mechanisms are confounded there [ARTIFACT:art_iYh9zVP7myjJ]. The geometry is correlational: pushing the grid task's states along the named map toward the survivors produced BFS in 300 of 300 programs [ARTIFACT:art_pHL7LWNhpcCS].

## 6 Discussion

The algorithm a code model writes behaves like a near-discrete decision taken at one or two tokens early in the program, and temperature acts on that decision only through the next-token distribution there. This single account explains the three regimes we observed. Where post-training has widened the fork margin to 5 to 17 nats, a temperature of 1.3 cannot reach the alternative, so the algorithm is fixed while every other position, where the next token is less certain, varies more; that is the phrasing growth of Figure 1. Where the forking token is contested, temperature sharpens or flattens the same two or three known algorithms at the rate the forking-token logits predict. And where the model reaches the decision through many openings, as Llama does on the grid task, the choice is spread over the opening and no single-token law captures it. In the terms of the question that motivates this work, a tight temperature with top-k 10 gives one idea in a few phrasings, and a loose one gives the same idea, or the same few ideas, in more phrasings.

This account reconciles two findings that look contradictory. Lee et al. report that temperature above 1 raises algorithmic diversity among correct programs [@Lee2025], and we find that temperature never changes the algorithm on default tasks. Both hold: on tasks whose fork is contested, temperature moves mass between known algorithms at the predicted rate (for example Prim on minimum spanning tree weight rises from 0.07 at T = 0.3 to 0.31 at T = 1.3), and on tasks whose fork is decided by several nats it does not. A diversity evaluation that pools tasks will see an average of the two. Our results also bear on the claim that a model returns the average answer and that only context moves it elsewhere. The instruct default is not the base model's average: post-training moved and sharpened one token, often promoting the base model's second or third choice, and left the repertoire unchanged.

For practice, the account says where to spend randomness. Temperature is a poor exploration control for algorithm choice, and its effect can be predicted before sampling from the forking-token logits. Controls that act upstream of the fork, such as context that implies an algorithm, a list-then-pick prompt, or perturbations of the task-specification states, do change the algorithm, but they move it to the runner-up the model already knows, and at a cost in correctness. The audits found no route from any single-sample control to a correct novel algorithm. An evaluator that keeps improvements across generations made the same 8B model better than the textbook rule on bin packing, which is where the field's discovery systems operate [@RomeraParedes2023; @Novikov2025]; whether it made the model new remains open after the replication found none.

For interpretability, the results suggest that pre-code readouts of a plan should be validated against the forking token. Natural language and sparse-feature readouts found no verbalised plan before the code, and fitted subspace edits at the fork moved the algorithm without passing the controls that would make them a variable of the model, consistent with the interpretability illusions that subspace patching can produce [@Makelov2023]. The forking token is where intervention is cheap and measurable, but a certified mechanism for the choice is still missing.

## 7 Limitations

Most results come from one model, Qwen3-8B, in non-thinking mode. The composed law was tested on three held-out units in two other families; two passed and Llama's grid task failed, below the four held-out units the pre-registered claim required, so the law's generality is an open question. The law was also not clearly better than a flat no-change baseline (four of six units, sign test p = 0.34), which means that much of its accuracy reflects how little temperature moves these units. The same-seed temperature null rests on 20 seeds per task, which bounds the per-seed change rate below 0.17 per task, not at zero.

The tasks are short, well-known programming problems whose solutions are likely memorised, with catalogues of three to ten known algorithms; the conclusions may not hold for open-ended programs or for problems without a textbook solution. Experiments ran on different engines (bfloat16 and FP8 linear layers, vLLM and Hugging Face); push escapes reproduced in bfloat16, but pushed cells showed precision sensitivity at the level of single streams. Phrasing clusters depend on a Jaccard threshold over identifier-normalised AST shingles, and the growth was driven mostly by the grid task.

Labels and the novelty audit carry their own uncertainty. Labellers were gated per task, but the gate failed by its strict criteria for the first decoding screen, and the expansion-order tracer used for the five-name ban failed its gold gate, so those numbers are descriptive. In the evaluator-guided search no LLM judge passed its control gate, so novelty there rests on manual reads, and one reader's eight candidates were not reproduced by the replication. The activation-space geometry is correlational, and the name-built map is confounded by lexical overlap between algorithm names.

## 8 Conclusion

In open-weight code models, temperature does not choose the algorithm; a forking token does, and temperature reaches the algorithm only through it. Under a shared random stream, the default algorithm survived every temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 in all 60 task-seeds we tested, while phrasings multiplied, and the fork margins that post-training wrote, 4.85 to 17.04 nats on the default tasks, account for the null. On contested forks, the forking-token logits committed before sampling predicted the temperature response within 0.014 to 0.054 total variation on five of six units. No control we tested produced a correct algorithm outside the known repertoire.

Future work follows directly:
- testing the composed law on more held-out units and families, including models that reach the fork through many openings;
- extending the forking-token analysis to reasoning traces, where the first approach named was fixed in every trace we read;
- spending sampling randomness at forking tokens inside evaluator-guided search, and measuring whether it buys ideas rather than phrasings;
- searching for a variable of the algorithm choice that passes label-permutation and random-initialisation controls.

Natural language and sparse-feature readouts found no verbalised plan before the code, and fitted subspace edits at the fork moved the algorithm without passing the controls that would make them a variable of the model, consistent with the interpretability illusions that subspace patching can produce [@Makelov2023]. The forking token is where intervention is cheap and measurable, but a certified mechanism for the choice is still missing.\n\n## 7 Limitations\n\nMost results come from one model, Qwen3-8B, in non-thinking mode.     num={k:i+1 for i,k in enumerate(keys)}
    def sub(m):
        ks=[k.strip().lstrip('@') for k in re.split(r';\s*', m.group(1))]
        return '['+', '.join(str(num[k]) for k in ks)+']'
    t2=re.sub(r'\[(@[^\]]+)\]', sub, t)
    refs='\n## References\n\n'+'\n'.join(f'[{num[k]}] {fmt(k)}' for k in keys)+'\n'
    open('paper_body_numbered.md','w').write(t2+refs)
    json.dump(num, open('citation_numbers.json','w'), indent=1)
    update_bib()
    open('../references.bib','w').write(bib)
    print(len(keys)); print(refs[:6000])

        o=''; depth=0; bt=False; j=0
        while j<len(s):
            c=s[j]

                if c in '([': depth+=1
                elif c in ')]': depth=max(0,depth-1)

Each has 40 to 48 seeded hidden test cases with per-case time limits and test-passing reference implementations of every catalogue algorithm [ARTIFACT:art__skdlFp_o3e9]. A further 13 tasks were derived from LeetCode problems with frozen wording and catalogues of 3 to 6 algorithms each, 684 hidden test cases in total, and references for all 54 catalogue algorithms [ARTIFACT:art_0ndRfWKBWclR]. The tasks used below are k-th smallest element (default: full sort), connected components (default: union-find), minimum spanning tree weight (Kruskal or Prim), trapped rain water (prefix and suffix maxima or two pointers) and valid anagram (sort and compare or counting), plus substring search and first and last position in a sorted array for Gemma. A *unit* is a task paired with one model. We call a unit a *default task* when the instruct model writes one algorithm in essentially all samples, and a *mixed unit* when its unperturbed samples already contain a second algorithm at a share of roughly 0.1 to 0.4.\n\nThe main model is Qwen3-8B [@Yang2025] in non-thinking mode unless stated, with Qwen3-8B-Base for the post-training comparison. gemma-3-4b-it [@Kamath2025] and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [@Grattafiori2024] supply held-out units, and Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking enabled enter the ban experiments. Generation used vLLM [@Kwon2023] or a Hugging Face engine in bfloat16 or with 8-bit floating-point (FP8) linear layers, stated per experiment.\n\nA program's *algorithm label* comes from a sandboxed runtime tracer that records queue, stack and heap operations, edge relaxations and grid reads, combined with AST rules; a blind LLM judge breaks disagreements. import re, statistics as st
t=open('paper_body_keys.md').read()

    p2=re.sub(r'\b(e\.g|i\.e|et al|vs)\.', lambda m: m.group(0).replace('.','<d>'), p)
    for s in re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z\(`"\*\[])', p2):
        if len(re.sub(r'\[ARTIFACT:[^\]]+\]','',s).split())>=3: sents.append(s.replace('<d>','.'))
L=sorted(len(re.sub(r'\[ARTIFACT:[^\]]+\]','',s).split()) for s in sents)
n=len(L); print('n',n,'median',st.median(L),'IQR',L[3*n//4]-L[n//4])
for s in sents:
    w=len(re.sub(r'\[ARTIFACT:[^\]]+\]','',s).split())
    if w>48: print(w,'||',s); print()

{"stdout": "## 1 Introduction\n\nAsk an instruction-tuned code model to implement a path search on a grid and it writes breadth-first search (BFS); ask it for a weighted shortest path and it writes Dijkstra's algorithm. The model knows the alternatives: when asked to list ten approaches before implementing one, Qwen3-8B names every grid algorithm in our catalogue in 100 of 100 lists [ARTIFACT:art_UoCVh2Qe5RZ0]. It simply does not use them. This paper asks which inference-time controls change the algorithm such a model implements, as opposed to the way it writes the same algorithm, and where inside generation that choice is made.\n\nThe question matters because many uses of code models depend on drawing different solutions rather than different spellings of one solution. Best-of-n sampling, program search with an automatic evaluator [@RomeraParedes2023; @Novikov2025] and creativity benchmarks [@Lu2024; @Zhang2025a] all assume that sampling explores the space of approaches. Output diversity is known to narrow after alignment, a pattern called generative monoculture [@Wu2024], and code models concentrate on a few algorithms among correct programs [@Lee2025; @Narula2026]. Sampling temperature is the control most often raised to counter this, and it is often described as the creativity parameter of a language model [@Peeperkorn2024].\n\nAnswering the question is harder than counting distinct outputs. Two programs can differ in every line and implement the same algorithm, and a program can name one algorithm while executing another, so labels must come from what the code does when run. Comparisons across temperatures drawn with independent random numbers mix the effect of temperature with sampling noise; with a default share near 1.0, a few stray samples look like a temperature effect. And knowing that an algorithm changes says nothing about where the decision was made: in the prompt representation, at some point during generation, or diffusely across the program.\n\nPrior work leaves these pieces apart. Algorithmic diversity has been measured across sampling settings with independent samples [@Lee2025], and the gap between strategy-level and surface-level diversity has been documented for mathematical reasoning [@Lee2026]. Forking tokens, positions where resampling changes the outcome distribution, have been found in text generation [@Bigelow2024], and post-training shifts are known to concentrate at a few high-entropy tokens [@Meng2026; @Wang2025]. No study we know of has located the token that decides which algorithm a code model writes, predicted from it what temperature will do before sampling, or measured temperature against an internal perturbation under one shared random stream.\n\nWe hold one random stream fixed per seed across conditions (common random numbers), label every program by its runtime behaviour on hidden tests, and locate forking tokens by prefix resampling. On three tasks where Qwen3-8B [@Yang2025] writes one default algorithm, sweeping temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 never changed the algorithm in any of 20 seeds per task, while the number of distinct phrasings grew. A random push of the prompt's task-specification activations changed it in most seeds on one task. The algorithm is settled at one or two forking tokens after a shared opening, and on the default tasks the default leads there by 4.85 to 17.04 nats, far more than temperature in the range 0.3 to 1.3 can overcome. Where the forking token is contested, a law composed from its teacher-forced logits predicts how temperature moves the mix. Our results cover one main model family, a small set of tasks, and a temperature law tested on only three held-out units, two of which passed.\n\n**Summary of contributions.**\n\n- **Temperature changes phrasings, not algorithms (Section 5.1).** Under a shared random stream, temperature 0.3 to 1.3 changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds on each of three tasks (pre-registered prediction, confirmed), while phrasing clusters per algorithm on the grid task rose from 3 to 13. On the same seeds a random task-state push (Section 3.3) changed it in 17.25 of 20 seeds on shortest path (paired difference 0.545, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.67). The null replicates with reasoning enabled (0 of 20 seeds) and over 800 independent samples per task.\n- **One or two forking tokens settle the algorithm (Section 5.2).** Given the class of the forking token, at most 0.19 bits of uncertainty about the algorithm remain; on four default tasks the fork margin is 4.85 to 17.04 nats.\n- **A composed forking-token law predicts temperature's effect (Section 5.3).** Committed before sampling, it matched the observed algorithm distribution across four temperatures within a mean total variation distance of 0.014 to 0.054 on five of six units, including two held-out Gemma-3-4B units, and failed on Llama-3.1-8B's grid task (0.142). A no-change baseline was close (the law was better on four of six units).\n- **The task-specification states and post-training set the fork (Section 5.4).** Writing the task-specification states of a prompt that names the minority algorithm into its padding twin produced that algorithm in 30 of 30 samples on each of three tasks. Post-training widened fork margins by 2.11 to 13.41 nats relative to the base model while changing the entropy at phrasing positions by less than 0.5 nats.\n- **Other controls reweight the same repertoire (Sections 5.5 and 5.6).** Random seeds, novelty instructions, bans, activation pushes and an evaluator-guided search moved programs among known algorithms. No audit found a correct novel algorithm, and where a five-name ban lands in activation space depends on whether the map is built from names or from programs.\n\nSection 2 places the work against prior studies, Section 3 describes the tasks, labels and interventions, Section 4 describes the protocol, Section 5 reports the results, and Sections 6 to 8 discuss them, state their limits and conclude.\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\n## 2 Related Work\n\n**Diversity collapse and creativity in code models.** Alignment narrows output diversity relative to the variety available for a task [@Wu2024; @Kirk2023], reduces conceptual diversity [@Murthy2025], and leaves base models better at randomness and creative generation than their aligned descendants [@West2025]. Chat-format structure alone contributes to this collapse [@Yun2025]. The typicality bias learned from human preferences has been linked to mode collapse that verbalized sampling partly undoes [@Zhang2025]. In code, Lee et al. find that models concentrate on few algorithms among correct solutions [@Lee2025], and Narula et al. show that subtle prompt cues steer which algorithm is chosen [@Narula2026]. Denial prompting, which forbids the technique of the previous solution, is used to measure creativity in code generation [@Lu2024]. Benchmarks of humanlike diversity [@Zhang2025a] and the distinction between approach-level and surface-level diversity in mathematical reasoning [@Lee2026] motivate counting ideas separately from phrasings. We adopt that separation for code, with ideas defined by runtime behaviour, and we measure it under coupled randomness so that the effect of a control on a single sample can be read directly.\n\n**Temperature and decoding.** Truncation samplers such as nucleus sampling [@Holtzman2019] and min-p sampling [@Nguyen2024] shape the token distribution at each step, and adaptive schemes raise temperature only where the next token is hard to predict [@Zhu2024; @Zhang2024]. Peeperkorn et al. find that temperature correlates only weakly with novelty in story generation [@Peeperkorn2024]. In code, Lee et al. report that temperature above 1 raises algorithmic diversity [@Lee2025], and Sohail and Ali observe more distinct operations in generated sorting algorithms as temperature rises from 0.75 to 1.1 [@Sohail2025]. Plan-level samplers diversify a sampled intent or plan before writing [@Ahmed2025; @Wang2024], and noise injected into embeddings or hidden states diversifies reasoning paths [@Kim2026; @Zhang2026]. Coupling counterfactual generations through shared Gumbel noise [@Ravfogel2024] is the closest precedent for our same-stream design. Our contribution is to explain why temperature does or does not reach the algorithm, and to predict the size of its effect from one token's logits before sampling.\n\n**Where an output is decided.** Forking Paths analysis resamples continuations from prefixes and finds tokens after which the outcome distribution changes abruptly [@Bigelow2024]. Thought anchors identify the reasoning sentences whose resampling matters most [@Bogdan2025]. And a small set of high-entropy minority tokens carries most of the effect of reinforcement learning on reasoning [@Wang2025]. Post-training shifts concentrate at a few tokens [@Meng2026], aligned models mostly reproduce the base model's top token at ordinary positions [@Lin2023], and learned behaviours can be enforced in the first few response tokens [@Qi2024]. Self-improvement and post-training have been described as sharpening probability onto outputs the base model already ranks highly [@Huang2024]. We extend this line to the algorithm a program implements: we locate its forking token blind, compose a temperature law over it, and measure how far post-training moved that token relative to ordinary positions.\n\n**Interventions on internal states and program search.** Activation steering adds a direction to the residual stream [@Rimsky2024; @Arditi2024], distributed alignment search fits subspaces in which interchange interventions reproduce a counterfactual [@Geiger2023; @Wu2023], and such subspace edits can act through pathways the model does not use naturally [@Makelov2023]. Representation geometry is studied with geodesic distances and Isomap [@Tenenbaum2000] and, recently, manifold steering [@Wurgaft2026]; sparse autoencoders [@Lieberum2024] and the tuned lens [@Belrose2023] read intermediate states. Evaluator-guided program search with a language model as mutator has found new constructions and heuristics [@RomeraParedes2023; @Novikov2025; @Liu2024; @Ye2024]. We use activation edits as tests of where the algorithm is set rather than as a diversity method, and we audit every correct program outside each task's catalogue for novelty.\n\n## 3 Method\n\nFigure 2 summarises the method. Programs are labelled by what they do when run (Section 3.1). Ideas are counted separately from phrasings (Section 3.2). Conditions are compared on shared random streams (Section 3.3). The token that decides the algorithm is located by prefix resampling (Section 3.4). A temperature law is composed from that token's logits (Section 3.5). And activation exchanges test what sets the token (Section 3.6).\n\n[FIGURE:fig2]", "stderr": "", "interrupted": false, "isImage": false, "noOutputExpected": false}

{"stdout": "### 3.1 Tasks, models and algorithm labels\n\nThe study starts from two path search tasks. In the grid task, `solve(grid, start, goal)` returns a valid path on a grid with walls; its catalogue holds BFS, depth-first search (DFS), bidirectional BFS, iterative deepening DFS, A* and unit-weight Dijkstra. The weighted shortest path task works on a directed graph, with a catalogue of Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford with its queue-based variant SPFA, bidirectional Dijkstra, Floyd-Warshall and Dial's algorithm. Each has 40 to 48 seeded hidden test cases with per-case time limits and test-passing reference implementations of every catalogue algorithm [ARTIFACT:art__skdlFp_o3e9]. A further 13 tasks were derived from LeetCode problems with frozen wording and catalogues of 3 to 6 algorithms each, 684 hidden test cases in total, and references for all 54 catalogue algorithms [ARTIFACT:art_0ndRfWKBWclR]. The tasks used below are k-th smallest element (default: full sort), connected components (default: union-find), minimum spanning tree weight (Kruskal or Prim), trapped rain water (prefix and suffix maxima or two pointers) and valid anagram (sort and compare or counting), plus substring search and first and last position in a sorted array for Gemma. A *unit* is a task paired with one model. We call a unit a *default task* when the instruct model writes one algorithm in essentially all samples, and a *mixed unit* when its unperturbed samples already contain a second algorithm at a share of roughly 0.1 to 0.4.\n\nThe main model is Qwen3-8B [@Yang2025] in non-thinking mode unless stated, with Qwen3-8B-Base for the post-training comparison. Held-out units come from gemma-3-4b-it [@Kamath2025] and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [@Grattafiori2024], and Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking enabled enter the ban experiments. Generation used vLLM [@Kwon2023] or a Hugging Face engine in bfloat16 or with 8-bit floating-point (FP8) linear layers, stated per experiment.\n\nA program's *algorithm label* comes from a sandboxed runtime tracer that records queue, stack and heap operations, edge relaxations and grid reads, combined with AST rules; a blind LLM judge breaks disagreements. Labellers were gated on references and adjudicated gold sets before use. On the bench tasks, agreement between the runtime and AST labellers reached Cohen's kappa 0.84 to 1.00, with every reference correctly labelled [ARTIFACT:art_0ndRfWKBWclR]. On the path tasks the combined label agreed with the adjudicated gold label at kappa 0.966 with 22 of 22 references correct, although the stricter runtime-against-AST criterion of that gate (kappa 0.753) was not met [ARTIFACT:art__skdlFp_o3e9]. A program is correct when it passes every hidden test.\n\n### 3.2 Ideas and phrasings\n\nWe call the runtime label of a correct program its *idea*. A *phrasing cluster* is a connected component, within one idea, of programs whose identifier-normalised AST 4-gram shingle sets have Jaccard similarity at least theta; identifiers are renamed in order of appearance, and comments, docstrings and constants are dropped. Theta 0.8 is primary, with 0.7 and 0.9 as sensitivity values [ARTIFACT:art_UoCVh2Qe5RZ0]. Diversity over ideas is the Hill number of order 1 (Hill-1), the exponential of the Shannon entropy of the idea distribution [@Hill1973], computed among correct programs and rarefied to a depth of 25 programs. The *number of ideas at depth 25* is the expected count of distinct ideas among 25 correct programs drawn from a cell.\n\n### 3.3 Same-stream sampling\n\nEvery comparison of decoding conditions samples by inverse-CDF sampling with common random numbers: each seed owns one stream of uniform variates, and every condition maps the same variates through its own next-token distribution. A difference between two conditions on one seed is therefore caused by the condition, not by a different draw. For a block of conditions, the *change count* of a task is the number of seeds whose algorithm label differs anywhere across the block; we bound its rate with the Clopper-Pearson interval [@Clopper1934]. Reasoning-mode arms ran in vLLM with per-request seeds, which couple conditions through a Gumbel-max race [@Ravfogel2024].\n\nThe temperature block ran each of 20 seeds per task (spread over five prompt templates) at T = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3 with top-p 1, and as sensitivity conditions with top-k 10 at T = 0.7 and with min-p 0.1 at T = 2.0 [ARTIFACT:art_Yu6GN6pLxW8f]. We call the comparison intervention a *random task-state push*. One isotropic unit direction is added, during the prefill only, to the residual stream activations at the token positions that state the task (the *task-specification states*) in blocks 12 to 23. Its size is set in multiples alpha of the displacement that a ban prompt induces at the same positions. Six fixed directions were run at alpha 1 and 2.\n\n### 3.4 Locating the forking token\n\nPrograms of different algorithms often share their first tokens; we call this common prefix the *shared opening*. Following Forking Paths analysis [@Bigelow2024], we sample base programs, resample continuations from their prefixes at increasing lengths, label every completed continuation, and detect a change point in the algorithm distribution with a pre-registered Bayesian rule calibrated against permutation nulls. The change point is refined to a single token and confirmed by forcing each candidate token and sampling continuations from it. When the branch after a forking token is not pure, a second forking token is searched inside it. We define the *fork margin* as the teacher-forced log-probability gap, at the forking token, between the class of tokens that lead to the default algorithm and the best class that leads elsewhere, and report H(A | class), the entropy of the algorithm given the forking token's class.\n\n### 3.5 A composed temperature law\n\nLet O_c be the c-th shared opening that precedes a forking token, and w_T(O_c) the probability of sampling it at temperature T, the product of tempered teacher-forced token probabilities along it. Let pi_T(t | O_c) be the tempered next-token distribution at the fork, renormalised over the top 10 logits for top-k 10, and P(A | t) the share of algorithm A among T = 1 continuations forced from token t. We call the prediction\n\nP_T(A) = sum_c w_T(O_c) [ sum_t pi_T(t | O_c) G(t, A) + r_T(c) P(A | rest_c) ] + (1 - sum_c w_T(O_c)) q_rest(A)\n\nthe *composed law*. Here G(t, A) = P(A | t) unless t opens a second fork, in which case G is the same mixture taken over the second fork's tokens. R_T(c) is the tempered mass outside the top 20 tokens and q_rest the composition of samples that leave the located openings. The prediction is averaged over five prompt templates and uses only teacher-forced logits and T = 1 conditionals, so it can be committed before any temperature sample is drawn [ARTIFACT:art_lzuosbrb34wB].\n\nFour rivals were committed with it: a flat law that keeps the T = 1 shares at every temperature, algorithm-level tempering that raises the T = 1 shares to the power 1/T and renormalises, a single-fork law without the second level, and the same law at the highest-entropy position instead of the located fork. Each predictor is scored by its mean absolute error (MAE), the mean over the four temperatures of the total variation distance between predicted and observed label distributions.\n\n### 3.6 Probing what sets the forking token\n\n*Task-state exchange.* A forced prompt (\"Implement the task with <minority algorithm>\") is paired with a *padding twin* in which the instruction is replaced by padding tokens so that all positions align. We write the forced prompt's task-specification states into the twin's forward pass and sample on shared streams, against a random exchange matched in norm [ARTIFACT:art_MZAfDPVhM6Ui].\n\n*Base against instruct.* Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-8B-Base are teacher-forced on identical chat-templated token ids, at the forking tokens and at 64 phrasing positions of 20 programs per task. We compare fork margins, next-token entropies and Jensen-Shannon divergences, and count how often the instruct model's token is the base model's top token, following the URIAL token categories [@Lin2023] [ARTIFACT:art_lzuosbrb34wB].\n\n### 3.7 Other controls and the novelty audit\n\nTo bound the result we also measured random context seeds (`seed=d32qxk4nt43` and `seed=(horse chair roof love)` prepended to the prompt) and a *semantic seed*, a paragraph that implies an algorithm without naming it. We further measured instructions from \"be creative\" to a 2,000-word request for a fully novel algorithm, bans of the default algorithm by name, bans of five algorithms at once, and an evaluator-guided island search in the manner of FunSearch [@RomeraParedes2023]. Every correct program labelled outside its task's catalogue was compared with a corpus of known solutions (about 18,000 programs built from LeetCode, textbook and benchmark solutions), read by blind LLM judges gated on known controls, and read manually. And where the model reaches the decision through many openings, as Llama does on the grid task, the choice is spread over the opening and no single-token law captures it. In the terms of the question that motivates this work, a tight temperature with top-k 10 gives one idea in a few phrasings, and a loose one gives the same idea, or the same few ideas, in more phrasings.\n\nThis account reconciles two findings that look contradictory. Lee et al. report that temperature above 1 raises algorithmic diversity among correct programs [@Lee2025], and we find that temperature never changes the algorithm on default tasks. Both hold. On tasks whose fork is contested, temperature moves mass between known algorithms at the predicted rate; Prim on minimum spanning tree weight rises from 0.07 at T = 0.3 to 0.31 at T = 1.3. On tasks whose fork is decided by several nats, it does not. A diversity evaluation that pools tasks will see an average of the two. Our results also bear on the claim that a model returns the average answer and that only context moves it elsewhere. The instruct default is not the base model's average: post-training moved and sharpened one token, often promoting the base model's second or third choice, and left the repertoire unchanged.\n\nFor practice, the account says where to spend randomness. Temperature is a poor exploration control for algorithm choice, and its effect can be predicted before sampling from the forking-token logits. Controls that act upstream of the fork, such as context that implies an algorithm, a list-then-pick prompt, or perturbations of the task-specification states, do change the algorithm, but they move it to the runner-up the model already knows, and at a cost in correctness. The audits found no route from any single-sample control to a correct novel algorithm. An evaluator that keeps improvements across generations made the same 8B model better than the textbook rule on bin packing, which is where the field's discovery systems operate [@RomeraParedes2023; @Novikov2025]. Whether it made the model new remains open after the replication found none.\n\nFor interpretability, the results suggest that pre-code readouts of a plan should be validated against the forking token. Natural language and sparse-feature readouts found no verbalised plan before the code, and fitted subspace edits at the fork moved the algorithm without passing the controls that would make them a variable of the model, consistent with the interpretability illusions that subspace patching can produce [@Makelov2023]. The forking token is where intervention is cheap and measurable, but a certified mechanism for the choice is still missing.\n\n## 7 Limitations\n\nMost results come from one model, Qwen3-8B, in non-thinking mode. The composed law was tested on three held-out units in two other families; two passed and Llama's grid task failed, below the four held-out units the pre-registered claim required, so the law's generality is an open question. The law was also not clearly better than a flat no-change baseline (four of six units, sign test p = 0.34), which means that much of its accuracy reflects how little temperature moves these units. The same-seed temperature null rests on 20 seeds per task, which bounds the per-seed change rate below 0.17 per task, not at zero.\n\nThe tasks are short, well-known programming problems whose solutions are likely memorised, with catalogues of three to ten known algorithms; the conclusions may not hold for open-ended programs or for problems without a textbook solution. Experiments ran on different engines (bfloat16 and FP8 linear layers, vLLM and Hugging Face); push escapes reproduced in bfloat16, but pushed cells showed precision sensitivity at the level of single streams. Phrasing clusters depend on a Jaccard threshold over identifier-normalised AST shingles, and the growth was driven mostly by the grid task.\n\nLabels and the novelty audit carry their own uncertainty. Labellers were gated per task, but the gate failed by its strict criteria for the first decoding screen, and the expansion-order tracer used for the five-name ban failed its gold gate, so those numbers are descriptive. In the evaluator-guided search no LLM judge passed its control gate, so novelty there rests on manual reads, and one reader's eight candidates were not reproduced by the replication. The activation-space geometry is correlational, and the name-built map is confounded by lexical overlap between algorithm names.\n\n## 8 Conclusion\n\nIn open-weight code models, temperature does not choose the algorithm; a forking token does, and temperature reaches the algorithm only through it. Under a shared random stream, the default algorithm survived every temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 in all 60 task-seeds we tested, while phrasings multiplied, and the fork margins that post-training wrote, 4.85 to 17.04 nats on the default tasks, account for the null. On contested forks, the forking-token logits committed before sampling predicted the temperature response within 0.014 to 0.054 total variation on five of six units. No control we tested produced a correct algorithm outside the known repertoire.\n\nFuture work follows directly:\n- testing the composed law on more held-out units and families, including models that reach the fork through many openings;\n- extending the forking-token analysis to reasoning traces, where the first approach named was fixed in every trace we read;\n- spending sampling randomness at forking tokens inside evaluator-guided search, and measuring whether it buys ideas rather than phrasings;\n- searching for a variable of the algorithm choice that passes label-permutation and random-initialisation controls.", "stderr": "", "interrupted": false, "isImage": false, "noOutputExpected": false}

# Paper draft: "Temperature Changes How a Code Model Writes, Not Which Algorithm It Chooses"

This directory holds the publishable paper written from the run's artifacts, as structured JSON for the
typesetting step (no LaTeX, no PDF, no image files are produced here).

## What it contains

The paper argues one finding: in open-weight code models, sampling temperature changes how a program is
written but not which algorithm it implements. Under a shared random stream, temperature 0.3 to 1.3 changed
Qwen3-8B's algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds on each of three default tasks (pre-registered, confirmed), while a random
push of the task-specification states changed it (paired difference 0.545, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.67). The algorithm
is settled at one or two forking tokens, and a law composed from their logits predicts temperature's effect on
contested units. Every number in the paper is taken from the output files of the run's artifacts and carries an
`[ARTIFACT:id]` marker naming the artifact it comes from.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|-|-|
| `.terminal_claude_agent_struct_out.json` | The deliverable: title, abstract, paper_text (markdown with `[FIGURE:id]` and `[ARTIFACT:id]` markers and a numbered reference list), figure specs, summary and the claim ledger (`headline_candidates`). |
| `references.bib`, `references.json` | Bibliography fetched from Semantic Scholar / OpenAlex by the `aii_semscholar_bib__fetch` script (51 cited entries plus fetch records); venues and years corrected to the published versions. |
| `notes/paper_body_keys.md` | Paper body with citation keys (`[@Key]`), the editable source of the text. |
| `notes/paper_body_numbered.md` | The same body with numbered citations and the reference list, as it appears in the JSON. |
| `notes/figures.json` | Specs of the five figures (four data figures with every plotted value, one concept diagram). |
| `notes/headline_candidates.json` | The claim ledger: one entry per candidate measurement, with outcome, comparator, interval and scope. |
| `notes/build_refs.py` | Numbers the citations by first appearance and writes the reference list. |
| `notes/assemble.py` | Assembles title, abstract, summary, body, figures and ledger into the output JSON. |
| `notes/bib_fetch_log.txt`, `notes/TODO.md` | Fetch log and the task checklist. |

## How to rebuild the output

```bash
cd notes
python3 build_refs.py      # numbers citations, writes paper_body_numbered.md
python3 assemble.py        # writes ../.terminal_claude_agent_struct_out.json
```

Both scripts use only the Python standard library.

## Restoring removed files

Nothing was marked for deletion: `.aii/manifest.yaml` has no entries, because the directory holds only text and
code below the 10 MB floor. The run's raw generations, labels and analysis outputs stay with the artifacts that
produced them and are not copied here.
EOF
echo done
````

We ask whether it changes which algorithm an open-weight code model implements, or only how the program is written, labelling every program by its runtime behaviour on hidden tests and holding one random stream fixed per seed across conditions. On three tasks where Qwen3-8B writes a single default algorithm (grid path search, weighted shortest path and k-th smallest element), raising temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds on every task, a pre-registered prediction that held (95% upper bound 0.17 per task) and replicated with reasoning enabled, while the number of distinct phrasings grew. On the same seeds, a random push of the prompt's task-specification states did change the algorithm, raising the per-seed change rate by a pre-registered paired difference of 0.545 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.67). Prefix resampling shows why: the algorithm is settled at one or two forking tokens, where the default leads by several nats that temperature cannot overcome, and post-training widened that lead. The algorithm is settled at one or two forking tokens whose logits predict temperature's small effect, so temperature multiplies phrasings rather than ideas, and no tested control produced a correct novel algorithm.\n\n# Temperature Changes How a Code Model Writes, Not Which Algorithm It Chooses\n\n## 1 Introduction\n\nAsk Qwen3-8B to implement a path search on a grid and it writes breadth-first search (BFS) in 99 of 100 programs; ask it for a weighted shortest path and it writes Dijkstra's algorithm in 100 of 100. The model knows the alternatives: when asked to list ten approaches before implementing one, Qwen3-8B names every grid algorithm in our catalogue in 100 of 100 lists [ARTIFACT:art_UoCVh2Qe5RZ0]. It simply does not use them. This paper asks which inference-time controls change the algorithm such a model implements, as opposed to the way it writes the same algorithm, and where inside generation that choice is made.\n\nThe question matters because many uses of code models depend on drawing different solutions rather than different spellings of one solution. Best-of-n sampling and program search with an automatic evaluator [1, 2] rely on sampling to explore the space of approaches, and creativity benchmarks measure how far it does [3, 4]. Output diversity is known to narrow after alignment, a pattern called generative monoculture [5], and code models concentrate on a few algorithms among correct programs [6, 7]. Sampling temperature is the control most often raised to counter this, and it is often described as the creativity parameter of a language model [8].\n\nAnswering the question is harder than counting distinct outputs. Two programs can differ in every line and implement the same algorithm, and a program can name one algorithm while executing another, so labels must come from what the code does when run. Comparisons across temperatures drawn with independent random numbers mix the effect of temperature with sampling noise; with a default share near 1.0, a few stray samples look like a temperature effect. And knowing that an algorithm changes says nothing about where the decision was made: in the prompt representation, at some point during generation, or diffusely across the program.\n\nPrior work leaves these pieces apart. Algorithmic diversity has been measured across sampling settings with independent samples [6], and the gap between strategy-level and surface-level diversity has been documented for mathematical reasoning [9]. Forking tokens, positions where resampling changes the outcome distribution, have been found in text generation [10], and post-training shifts are known to concentrate at a few high-entropy tokens [11, 12]. No study we know of has located the token that decides which algorithm a code model writes, predicted from it what temperature will do before sampling, or measured temperature against an internal perturbation under one shared random stream.\n\nWe hold one random stream fixed per seed across conditions (common random numbers), label every program by its runtime behaviour on hidden tests, and locate forking tokens by prefix resampling. On three tasks where Qwen3-8B [13] writes one default algorithm, sweeping temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 never changed the algorithm in any of 20 seeds per task, while the number of distinct phrasings grew (Figure 1). A random push of the prompt's task-specification states changed it in most seeds on one task. The algorithm is settled at one or two forking tokens after a shared opening, and on the default tasks the default leads there by 4.85 to 17.04 nats, far more than temperature in the range 0.3 to 1.3 can overcome. Where the forking token is contested, a law composed from its teacher-forced logits predicts how temperature moves the mix. Our results cover one main model family, a small set of tasks, and a temperature law tested on only three held-out units, two of which passed.\n\n**Summary of contributions.**\n\n- **Temperature changes phrasings, not algorithms (Section 5.1).** Under a shared random stream, temperature 0.3 to 1.3 changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds on each of three tasks (pre-registered prediction, confirmed), while phrasing clusters per algorithm on the grid task rose from 3 to 13. On the same seeds a random task-state push (Section 3.3) changed it in 17.25 of 20 seeds on shortest path (paired difference 0.545, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.67). The null replicates with reasoning enabled (0 of 20 seeds) and over 800 independent samples per task.\n- **One or two forking tokens settle the algorithm (Section 5.2).** Given the class of the forking token, at most 0.19 bits of uncertainty about the algorithm remain; on four default tasks the fork margin is 4.85 to 17.04 nats.\n- **A composed forking-token law predicts temperature's effect (Section 5.3).** Committed before sampling, it matched the observed algorithm distribution across four temperatures within a mean total variation distance of 0.014 to 0.054 on five of six units, including two held-out Gemma-3-4B units, and failed on Llama-3.1-8B's grid task (0.142). In code, Lee et al. find that models concentrate on few algorithms among correct solutions [6], and Narula et al. show that subtle prompt cues steer which algorithm is chosen [7]. Denial prompting, which forbids the technique of the previous solution, is used to measure creativity in code generation [3]. Benchmarks of humanlike diversity [4] and the distinction between approach-level and surface-level diversity in mathematical reasoning [9] motivate counting ideas separately from phrasings. Plan-level samplers diversify a sampled intent or plan before writing [24, 25], random embeddings injected into the input diversify reasoning paths [26], and the level at which randomness enters a generation pipeline changes how diverse its outputs are [27]. ```
I've written the paper and saved it as the structured JSON at `./.terminal_claude_agent_struct_out.json`, along with `references.bib` (51 entries, all fetched by the bib script), `README.md` and `.aii/manifest.yaml`. Nothing in the workspace is large enough to need a manifest entry, so the manifest has none.

**Title:** "Temperature Changes How a Code Model Writes, Not Which Algorithm It Chooses"

**Headline (pre-registered, passed).** I picked this by evidence strength: it is the most-replicated finding and its test was pre-registered.
- Qwen3-8B was given one fixed random stream per seed. Sweeping temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds on each of three tasks (grid path, shortest path, k-th smallest). The exact upper bound is 0.17 per task.
- Over the same sweep, the number of distinct phrasings grew; on the grid task it went from 3 to 13.
- On the same seeds, a random push of the prompt's task-specification states changed the algorithm far more often. The pre-registered paired difference is 0.545 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.67).
- The result holds with reasoning switched on (0 of 20 seeds, including with top-k 10) and over 800 independent samples per task.

**Supporting results:**
- **Where the choice is made:** one or two early tokens settle the algorithm, leaving at most 0.19 bits of uncertainty. On the tasks where the model always writes one algorithm, that algorithm leads at the deciding token by 4.85 to 17.04 nats, more than temperature can overcome.
- **Predicting temperature's effect:** a rule built from the logits at that token was committed before sampling. It predicted how temperature shifts the mix of algorithms on 5 of 6 units, including 2 held-out units in Gemma-3-4B.
- **Post-training:** compared with the base model, the instruct model's lead at the deciding token is 2.11 to 13.41 nats wider, while ordinary positions barely changed.
- **Novelty:** no control produced a correct novel algorithm.

**Caveats the paper states:**
- The prediction rule's overall verdict is partial. Only 3 held-out units were scored where 4 were required, the Llama unit failed, and a "temperature changes nothing" baseline was nearly as accurate (better on 4 of 6 units, p 0.34).
- The headline temperature runs used 8-bit layers.
- Some labellers failed their accuracy checks, so those numbers are reported as descriptive only.
- The activation-space geometry is correlational. Whether the five-algorithm ban lands "at the edge or opposite" depends on whether the map is built from algorithm names or from programs.

The paper is organised by idea, not by iteration. It has a main results table and five figures: four plot real numbers, one is a method diagram. Figure 1 shows the headline. All 31 artifact ids in the markers check against the run's list, and the citations in the text match the reference list one for one. It addresses every item in your original request, including the 1a–c temperature question, context seeds, novelty instructions, NLA, SAE, DAS, circuits, the logit and Jacobian lenses, and the top-five ban map in activation space.

Sources used in the last related-work search:
- [Towards a Measure of Algorithm Similarity (arXiv 2510.27063)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.27063)
- [Beyond the 80/20 Rule (arXiv 2506.01939)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.01939)
- [Hot or Cold? Adaptive Temperature Sampling for Code Generation (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/27798)

I can also publish the draft as a private page to read or share if that's useful.

### 5.1 A task-state push changes the algorithm where temperature does not

On the same random streams, a random task-state push changed Qwen3-8B's algorithm in more seeds than temperature did, by a paired difference of 0.545 per seed (95% bootstrap CI 0.41 to 0.67), pooled over shortest path and k-th smallest (40 seeds; Figure 1 and Table 1) [ARTIFACT:art_Yu6GN6pLxW8f]. The contrast is the push's change count for a seed, a union over three directions at alpha 1 and T = 1.0, minus the seed's change count across the four temperatures. It was pre-registered as the experiment's single entry in the secondary test family and held, with a one-sided sign-flip p of 1.0e-5. A within-seed permutation of conditions never reaches the observed mean (maximum placebo mean 0.155 in 200 permutations). The experiment as a whole is graded partial: its pre-registered prediction that the push changes at least 5 of 20 seeds held on shortest path (17.25) but failed on k-th smallest (4.55). The contrast was run only in the 8-bit (FP8 W8A8) engine and was not rerun in bfloat16. The push itself does reproduce in bfloat16 at the same absolute dose unit (Section 4).

**Table 1.** Seeds (of 20) whose algorithm changes across the conditions of a block, Qwen3-8B, same random stream per seed, 8-bit W8A8 engine except the thinking-mode arm (vLLM). Push rows are the mean over the 20 three-direction subsets of six fixed directions of the number of seeds whose label differs anywhere among the unpushed arm and the three directions.

| Conditions on the same seeds | Shortest path (Dijkstra) | k-th smallest (full sort) | Grid path (BFS) |
|-|-|-|-|
| Temperature 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, top-p 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| The same, plus top-k 10 at T 0.7 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| The same, plus min-p 0.1 at T 2.0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| Temperature 0.3 to 1.3, thinking mode | 0 | not run | 0 (of 10) |
| Random task-state push, alpha 1, T 1.0 | 17.25 | 4.55 | 2.50 |
| Random task-state push, alpha 2, T 1.0 | 19.05 | 10.60 | 8.70 |

A single push direction at alpha 1 changed 7, 10, 15, 17, 3 and 8 of 20 seeds on shortest path and up to 7 of 20 on k-th smallest. The algorithms the changed programs moved to, their *landings*, were Bellman-Ford/SPFA (52 of 60 off-default programs on shortest path) and quickselect (11 of 11 on k-th smallest). The push is not free: pass rates on shortest path fell from 1.00 to 0.63 at alpha 1 and 0.42 at alpha 2.

Temperature, on the same seeds, never changed the algorithm on any of the three default tasks. Across T = 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3, all 20 seeds kept their algorithm on shortest path (Dijkstra), on k-th smallest (full sort) and on the grid task (BFS). The change count is 0 of 20 per task, with an exact 95% upper bound of 0.168 on the per-seed change rate. This was a separate pre-registered prediction (at most 1 of 20 seeds per cell), and it held under every reading: counting only correct programs, counting invalid outputs as a label, and adding top-k 10 as a fifth condition all leave the count at 0. Adding min-p 0.1 at T = 2.0 changes one seed on shortest path and one on k-th smallest. With thinking mode enabled, shortest path kept Dijkstra in 20 of 20 seeds, every final program and every first approach named in the reasoning was Dijkstra, and all 100 traces completed within the 16k-token cap. The reduced grid arm kept BFS in 10 of 10 seeds.

[FIGURE:fig1]

Phrasings, in contrast, grow with temperature (Figure 3). On the grid task the number of phrasing clusters among 20 programs rose from 3 at T = 0.3 to 10, 12 and 13 at T = 0.7, 1.0 and 1.3, while the number of distinct algorithms stayed at 1 on all three tasks at every temperature. The pooled slope of log phrasings per idea on temperature is 0.70 per unit T (95% CI 0.35 to 0.93) at Jaccard threshold 0.8, and 0.64 [0.30, 0.89] and 0.81 [0.33, 0.98] at 0.7 and 0.9. Almost all of the growth comes from the grid task, while shortest path moves from 1 to 2 clusters and k-th smallest stays at 2.

[FIGURE:fig3]

The temperature null replicates outside the seed-coupled design and the 8-bit engine. With 100 independent samples per cell, 797 of 800 grid programs were BFS and 797 of 800 shortest path programs were Dijkstra across eight temperature and sampler cells in non-thinking mode, and 800 of 800 in thinking mode [ARTIFACT:art_UoCVh2Qe5RZ0]. Over the same cells, grid phrasing clusters at threshold 0.8 rose from 4 to 36 with top-k 10 and from 3 to 24 with top-p 0.95. The literal setting of thinking mode with top-k 10 under one seed per stream again changed the shortest path algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds (one-sided 95% upper bound 0.139) [ARTIFACT:art_jR6Pyy3W9xum], and in bfloat16, 100 samples at T = 1.3 from the forking position left the default unchanged on four tasks (Section 5.2). At tight temperature the model therefore writes one idea in a few phrasings, and loosening temperature multiplies the phrasings of that idea rather than adding ideas.

Which default a model writes depends on the model.
